that the engine reported for that token when it reaches the policy loss.

We connected the non-agentic async runner to the existing direct model client,
preserving native token IDs and behavior logprobs. We also made policy-version
stamping conservative across weight updates and covered grouped admission,
backpressure, failure, and cancellation behavior. This avoided using text
retokenization as a substitute for the sampled sequence.

The result was a CPU-tested path suitable for real Megatron qualification, without
changing vLLM’s implementation or the training objective.

Next at this milestone: verify the objective and weight-transfer path on H100s.

Evidence: [direct client](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/001f6691aec4ee3beb16d2d82feac6eea73fd5eb/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/trajectory_runners/model_clients.py#L26);
[rollout version capture](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/001f6691aec4ee3beb16d2d82feac6eea73fd5eb/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/trajectory_runners/skyrl_gym.py#L303).

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 **Pass the model-level Megatron hardware gates**

Before relying on a full training run, we checked two narrower questions on H100s:
does Megatron perform the intended update with the selected PPO loss, `behavior_clip`, and can it publish updated
weights to separate inference workers?

The objective/update test passed against an independent reference, including timing
instrumentation off/on parity. The weight-transfer test initially reached broadcast
but lacked its validation dataset; after preparing that fixture, the transfer and
inference test passed as well.

This established the model-level prerequisites. It did not yet prove the full async
loop, tracker lifecycle, checkpoint/export pipeline, or a throughput advantage.

Next at this milestone: exercise the complete Marin-orchestrated runner.

Evidence: [hardware tests in the implementation checkpoint](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/commit/de13e146bca46bd04f1f040f3807b081497ce237).
Hardware results: objective gate passed; corrected weight-sync gate **1 passed in
159.61 seconds**, Iris succeeded.

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 **Give async execution its own timing and work accounting**

The observability mandate was to diagnose where time and generated work go while
many rollouts overlap. Summing overlapping rollout walls into a synchronous
“generate” phase would produce misleading timings.

We added per-call rollout timing, concurrent wait counters, queue/dwell/staleness
observations, group/token outcomes, event-loop lag, and explicit policy drains and
weight-publication phases. Policy drains measure waits for policy workers to reach
a synchronization point. Megatron received worker-side phase timing. Signed residuals
(parent wall minus exclusive child phases) expose accounting errors; process, rank,
step, and attempt identities keep unrelated observations separate.

CPU serialization, failure, concurrency, and accounting checks passed. The resulting
telemetry can distinguish useful consumed work from speculative work that is discarded.

Next at this milestone: verify the emitted records manually against actual training runs.

Evidence: [rollout observations](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/001f6691aec4ee3beb16d2d82feac6eea73fd5eb/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollout_observability.py#L182);
[Megatron implementation](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/001f6691aec4ee3beb16d2d82feac6eea73fd5eb/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/workers/megatron/megatron_worker.py).

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 **Complete the synchronous end-to-end control**

The first full-run mandate was to establish a reproducible control through Marin:
regional input preparation, training, checkpointing, HF export, and evaluation.

The pinned fixture contained 1,024 training and 128 validation rows with disjoint
source IDs. Startup attempts exposed attention-backend and microbatch constraints;
we selected the supported fused-attention path and matched forward/train microbatches.
The successful control used eight policy and eight inference H100s.

It completed four optimizer updates and export/evaluation. Manual Finelog checks
verified **1,024 consumed sequences and 159,233 generated = consumed tokens**, with
all seven Megatron phases on all eight policy ranks at all four steps. This proved
the full pipeline; a remaining W&B terminal-state defect became the next task.

Next at this milestone: make tracker and process lifecycle equally reliable for sync and async.

Evidence: [sync control in W&B](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/n7wtf7vi).
This historical tracker later showed `crashed` despite successful Iris training;
the following milestone addresses that discrepancy.

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 **Make W&B and Finelog agree on steps and completion**

Step-level W&B tracking was a requirement alongside Finelog, with the entity supplied
by launch configuration rather than hardcoded in the experiment.

We fixed shared-mode W&B logging to use an explicit global-step axis, commit each
training step, and finish with the training exit status. Investigation also found
that the async entrypoint bypassed the common experiment lifecycle, leaving worker
timings visible while trainer telemetry was missing. It now uses the shared lifecycle,
and evaluation scalars are mirrored into Finelog.

Success and failure lifecycle regressions passed. The corrected async runs subsequently
had **finished W&B histories with steps 1–4**, matching direct Finelog queries.

Next at this milestone: qualify the complete async pipeline under two freshness settings.

Evidence: [tracker implementation](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/001f6691aec4ee3beb16d2d82feac6eea73fd5eb/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/utils/tracking.py#L93);
[lifecycle repair](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/commit/534dc5d2bb77d6c9e198754bbef24f99c7045e4e).

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 **Complete async smokes with staleness limits 1 and 0**

The mandate was to establish real async functionality and freshness accounting,
before claiming performance. We ran matched four-update configurations with allowed
staleness 1 and 0, measured in completed policy updates; both completed training,
checkpoint/export, and terminal evaluation.
Each consumed **1,024 sequences** on 16 H100s.

| Token ledger | Staleness limit 1 | Staleness limit 0 |
|---|---:|---:|
| Generated response tokens | 195,522 | 158,043 |
| Consumed response/loss tokens | 158,148 | 158,043 |
| Discarded response tokens | 37,374 | 0 |

Both ledgers reconciled, observed consumed lag respected the configured bound, and
no nonfinite training values or telemetry loss were reported. A stale terminal queue
gauge exposed by this audit was then fixed and regression-tested.

Neither rollout completions nor recorded model-await intervals overlapped the
measured optimizer-training intervals in the small workload. Replacement generation
finished during learner preparation, before the optimizer phase. This describes the
recorded driver intervals; these functional smokes did not establish a speedup or
learning-quality result.

Next at this milestone: make these measurements easy to inspect and compare over longer sessions.

Evidence: [staleness-1 run](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/gl4sy92i),
[staleness-0 run](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/bjm39ire);
[queue-gauge repair](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/commit/663d88d20f71c6b0ac4fe1be586c76772b54c7ac).

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 **Put real async telemetry in Grafana**

The dashboard mandate was a companion to Marin’s existing synchronous RL view,
with enough detail to diagnose the async producer/consumer relationship.

We added **Async RL Training**, initially with 21 panels covering progress, useful
work, queues, waits, staleness, policy/weight timings, overlap, quality, rank detail,
and exporter health. Filters preserve run/job/execution identity, and missing or
window-clipped observations remain distinguishable from measured zero.

The initial dashboard passed **77 SQL/provisioning tests**. Every panel and query
selector was also executed against live Finelog, and browser checks confirmed real
run data. Production deployment has not been performed.

Next at this milestone: extend the view with policy-probability drift and resource-normalized throughput.

Evidence: [dashboard source](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3febf6b056f2a7903210dc91bc15f72fd3f1fe39/infra/grafana/dashboards/async_rl.json#L1).

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 **Measure off-policy distance and useful work per resource**

The next mandate was to separate two questions: how many policy versions old is a
rollout, and how differently does the learner score the actual sampled tokens?

We added full-batch diagnostics for **pre-update learner logprob minus reported
behavior logprob** on finite loss tokens: coverage, signed/absolute log-ratio summaries,
tails, clipping-window pressure, and token-weight concentration. These reuse the
existing learner forward. We also added topology/batch metadata and consumed-token
rates normalized by configured policy/inference GPU counts. Core time excludes
callbacks; cycle time includes checkpoint/evaluation work up to metric publication.
Both exclude startup, epoch cleanup, and final export.

The dashboard grew to **29 panels**, with the new scalars also in W&B and Finelog.
Direct queries verified real values. A zero-version-lag Qwen batch still had mean
absolute log-ratio **0.01198**. This is a scoring discrepancy even without policy
aging; inference/training numerical differences are possible contributors whose
individual effects have not been isolated. These diagnostic ratios are not a KL
estimate or an established safe staleness threshold.

Next at this milestone: test their behavior across 100 updates and repeated epoch transitions.

Evidence: [drift calculation](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/001f6691aec4ee3beb16d2d82feac6eea73fd5eb/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/utils/importance_ratio_diagnostics.py#L27),
[resource/time denominators](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/001f6691aec4ee3beb16d2d82feac6eea73fd5eb/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollout_observability.py#L45),
[Qwen measurements](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/t4mom8ql).

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 **Qualify a 100-update Qwen session**

The endurance mandate was to move beyond startup smokes while retaining the simple
Qwen/GSM8K, Megatron, eight-policy/eight-inference configuration.

The run completed **100 optimizer updates, publications 0–100, six epoch transitions,
and 25,600 consumed sequences**. Checkpoints ran every 25 updates and evaluation
every 10. Training, final HF export, and the separate terminal evaluation all succeeded;
W&B finished with all 100 training rows manually verified.

Finelog reconciled **6,690,949 generated tokens = 6,536,199 consumed + 154,750 discarded**.
All steps had finite drift diagnostics and one optimizer update, consumed lag remained
within 1, and the final queue was empty with no reported exporter loss.

This establishes a working longer-session baseline. Answers grew longer late in
training, and callback/epoch overhead remained visible, so endurance alone does not
establish an optimal resource split or an async speed advantage.

Next at this milestone: run a controlled 20-update sync/async comparison and qualify Snowball separately.

Evidence: [finished Qwen100 run](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/t4mom8ql);
[qualification schedule](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3febf6b056f2a7903210dc91bc15f72fd3f1fe39/experiments/post_training/async_rl.py#L99).

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 **Establish the first matched sync/async timing result**

The comparison mandate was to measure whether async completes equivalent training
work faster. Both arms used the same source, initial Qwen checkpoint, 1,536-row
fixture, optimizer/batch settings, seed, and **8 policy + 8 inference H100s** in the
same cluster. Each update consumed 64 prompts × 4 responses = 256 sequences.
Twenty updates stayed within one epoch, with evaluation/checkpointing only at update
20. Dispatch order and sampled trajectories can still differ.

We measured from initial weight publication through publication after update 20,
including rollout fill and interstep overhead, excluding setup and final callbacks.

| Measurement | Sync | Async |
|---|---:|---:|
| Optimizer updates / consumed sequences | 20 / 5,120 | 20 / 5,120 |
| Training-window time | 252.7 s | 320.8 s |
| Consumed response/loss tokens | 823,760 | 819,746 |
| Consumed tokens per second | 3,259.8 | 2,555.6 |
| Allocated GPU-hours in that window | 1.123 | 1.426 |

Async took **26.9% longer** and delivered **21.6% fewer consumed tokens per GPU-hour**.
Token counts differed by only 0.49%, and excluding the first two updates preserved
the finding. Both trackers finished with complete, finite step metrics.

The scheduled 128-example evaluation at update 20 scored **87/128 for sync and
79/128 for async**. A separate training-end callback repeated evaluation at the same
weights and also favored sync (89/128 versus 78/128). This single stochastic pair
does not establish a general quality effect. Both arms also completed HF export and
the separate terminal evaluation stage.

This is a useful calibration point for the epic: the current small-model configuration
has measurable overhead to address. It does not determine Snowball’s result or the
performance/quality tradeoff at other resource and freshness settings.

Next at this milestone: identify the costs behind the gap before changing GPU allocation.

Evidence: [sync run](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/xopx415q),
[async run](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/276c1nmj);
[comparison preset](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3febf6b056f2a7903210dc91bc15f72fd3f1fe39/experiments/post_training/async_rl.py#L99).

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 **Explain the measured publication bottleneck**

The follow-up mandate was to distinguish weight communication from the other work
inside the synchronization timer.

In the 20-update pair, weight publication cost **48.79 seconds for sync versus
147.40 seconds for async**, including **100.55 seconds of async pause time**.
The client unconditionally waits five seconds before pausing inference schedulers.
Meanwhile, sync’s entire generation phase cost only **35.87 seconds** across the run.
Async’s admission wait totaled 1.96 seconds: a 33.91-second reduction relative to
sync generation. Publication added 98.61 seconds, and the combined learner/logprob
phases added 0.56 seconds. These separately measured components account for 65.27
of the 68.06-second slowdown. The pause is already included in publication time.
This finding does not establish a slower network.

Publication happens after each optimizer update: Megatron reconstructs model
parameters and sends them **trainer → inference**, one parameter at a time. Gradients
and rollout logprobs are outside this transfer. The Qwen transfer crosses the policy/
inference node boundary; its retained logs do not establish the selected NCCL transport.

We also identified synchronous DataLoader worker startup at evaluation/epoch boundaries,
matching recurring ~30-second event-loop stalls, and duplicate final evaluation from
two callbacks. These sit outside the comparison’s primary timing window. Precise loader
cost attribution still needs dedicated timing.

Next at this milestone: test a correctness-preserving pause handshake, then rerun the control. Later
experiments can vary publication cadence, allowed lag, and GPU split; changing
`max_staleness_steps` alone currently does not change publication frequency.

Evidence: [pause implementation](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/001f6691aec4ee3beb16d2d82feac6eea73fd5eb/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/inference_engines/inference_engine_client.py#L850),
[parameter publication](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/001f6691aec4ee3beb16d2d82feac6eea73fd5eb/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/workers/megatron/megatron_worker.py#L739),
[DataLoader setup](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/001f6691aec4ee3beb16d2d82feac6eea73fd5eb/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/utils/trainer_utils.py#L503),
[evaluation callbacks](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/blob/001f6691aec4ee3beb16d2d82feac6eea73fd5eb/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/callbacks/builtin.py#L149).

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 **Prepare and launch the first Snowball qualification gate**

The next-model mandate is Megatron training of Snowball, the 67B-A2B mixture-of-experts
model, followed by sufficiently long runs to study resource balance and off-policy
tradeoffs.

We added separate two-update and 25-update presets around the existing regional
67B-A2B SFT export. The policy uses **32 H100s** with tensor parallelism 1, pipeline parallelism 2, and
expert parallelism 8; inference uses another **8 H100s** on one node. The export’s thinking template is retained, and host-memory/
disk requests account for Megatron checkpoint staging.

A regional CPU audit passed on all **1,024 training and 128 validation prompts** using
the actual export tokenizer: training prompts were 113–261 tokens, validation prompts
115–216. Both configurations passed full launcher/trainer validation. After capacity
became available, the **40-H100 two-update gate was admitted**. NCCL initialization
logging is enabled to inspect transport selection.

This milestone is model/configuration readiness and a launched gate. Snowball training
and the 25-update run are **not yet qualified**.

Next at this milestone: verify forward/backward, useful rewards, weight publication and subsequent
rollouts, checkpoint/export, and output-limit behavior before launching the longer run.

Evidence: [Snowball recipe and tokenizer audit](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3febf6b056f2a7903210dc91bc15f72fd3f1fe39/experiments/post_training/async_snowball.py#L83).
Iris coordinator: `/atqamar/async-rl-snowball-gate-coordinator-v1`.

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 Snowball completes two async updates

Snowball 67B-A2B now completes two async Megatron updates on 32 learner + 8 rollout H100s, including weight publication and checkpoint saving. [W&B](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/gxwqg87k) is finished with both steps recorded.

The first attempt exposed a gradient-buffer restore without a preceding offload. We replaced the manual storage handling with Megatron's native buffer lifecycle and rejected the unsupported async optimizer-offload setting. A one-H100 numerical regression passed before repeating the Snowball gate. [Repair](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/commit/e59c2e90bfb6a9664304ad13a760e6da55ceec1a).

The run consumed 256 responses and 127,786 tokens. Finelog reconciles 191,440 generated tokens = 127,786 consumed + 63,654 discarded at shutdown. Consumed weight-version lag was zero at update 1 and one at update 2; the recorded probability diagnostics were finite throughout.

Three observations set the next experiment:

- 81.25% of consumed responses at update 1 and 82.03% at update 2 hit the 512-token limit, with complete stop-reason coverage. The next run uses the planned 2,048-token per-response limit and measures this fraction again. Length stops alone do not establish answer incompleteness.
- Update 2 took 31.17 seconds of core training time, including 19.84 seconds of weight synchronization (63.6%) and about 4 milliseconds waiting for rollouts. Two updates are insufficient to choose a GPU split; longer Snowball measurements come first.
- Final checkpoint saving added about 554 seconds. We will report core throughput and checkpoint-inclusive completion time separately.

The new consumed-length metrics reached W&B but were omitted by Finelog's scalar filter. That filter is fixed for subsequent runs, and the Grafana dashboard now has a length-stop/coverage panel. Historical missing values remain gaps.

Automated export is currently blocked by Iris marking the head pod deleted after its successful driver exit. Next: recover conversion of the saved checkpoint to Hugging Face format, completing the model artifact needed by downstream consumers. Then start a fresh 25-update run from the original SFT model, evaluating the same held-out set before training and at update 25. This gate establishes training functionality; it does not establish a quality gain, a speed advantage, or the optimal allocation.

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 Snowball checkpoint export completes; 25-update qualification submitted

The checkpoint from Snowball’s two-update gate now loads and exports successfully. Export-only recovery on 32 H100s finished all four tasks with exit 0, zero failures and zero preemptions, followed by portable HF artifact verification. This recovers the artifact; the original training coordinator’s completion failure remains a separate orchestration result.

An earlier recovery attempt exposed a scaling problem: each of 32 policy workers would download the entire 939 GB checkpoint. Staging once per node reduced that to four validated copies. Each contained 45 objects and 939.3 GB, taking 17.6–19.1 minutes per node. The successful export tasks took about 33 minutes overall. This checkpoint/export cost sits outside the training-update timing window. The repair is in [MSR133bb554](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/commit/133bb5541eb61c2f65f077195ee907efc38fe144), pinned by [Marin8250cfb3e1](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/8250cfb3e1d92726028052da418f74dbb24f90fc).

Decision: proceed to 25-update Snowball qualification. The coordinator is submitted as `async-rl-snowball25-coordinator-v1` after checking H100 capacity. It starts from the original SFT model, uses 32 learner + 8 rollout GPUs, raises the response limit to 2,048 tokens, and evaluates the same 128 held-out prompts before and after training. Checkpointing remains at the final update because the gate’s save took roughly nine minutes. The next result should establish whether training and telemetry remain stable over longer responses and identify the next resource-allocation or publication-schedule experiment. It does not yet establish an optimal GPU split or an acceptable policy-lag range.

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 Snowball completes 25 async updates; publication cadence is the next control

Snowball completed 25 async Megatron updates on 32 learner + 8 rollout H100s, using GSM8K, GRPO, and a 2,048-token response limit. All five training tasks exited successfully with no retries or preemptions. [W&B](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/vupc3ir9) is finished with 25 finite training rows; direct Finelog queries verified publications 0–25, an empty terminal rollout buffer, and zero reported telemetry loss.

| Measurement | Result |
|---|---:|
| Core training-loop time, all 25 updates | 948.3 s |
| Updates 2–25: weight publication / training / rollout waiting | 56.2% / 21.9% / 21.4% of their 866.5 s core time |
| Final checkpoint saving | 547.3 s, outside core time |
| Consumed responses / response tokens | 3,200 / 3,312,485 |
| Generated tokens discarded as stale / terminal surplus | 7.52% / 3.32% |
| Consumed responses reaching the token limit | 17.44% |

The generated-token ledger closes exactly: 3,715,171 = 3,312,485 consumed + 279,441 stale + 123,245 terminal surplus. Core timing excludes evaluation, checkpointing, startup, and export; it is not the complete job runtime.

On the same 128 held-out prompts, greedy evaluation rose from 99/128 (77.3%) initially to 116/128 (90.6%) at update 25. The existing shutdown path repeated evaluation with the same final weights and scored 117/128 (91.4%). Keep these as two observations of the same checkpoint, without pooling them. This establishes a completed 25-update baseline; it does not establish a safe range of policy lag.

Consumed policy age stayed within one optimizer update. The token importance-weight ESS fraction stayed between 0.9909 and 0.9930; this drift diagnostic does not replace held-out evaluation.

Next, add a controlled weight-publication interval, preserving separate learner and installed-weight identities and measuring lag in optimizer updates. Validate the current every-update behavior, then gate an every-two-updates run before a matched 25-update comparison. Hold the other training and inference settings fixed, with a consistent initial/final evaluation schedule. Publication dominates the measured loop, so this is the next performance/quality experiment. A 16-learner-GPU control still needs a memory and full-update gate. vLLM optimization remains in its separate workstream.

Automatic HF export of update 25 is running. Sources: [MarinSkyRL 133bb554](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/commit/133bb5541eb61c2f65f077195ee907efc38fe144), [Marin 8250cfb3](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/8250cfb3e1d92726028052da418f74dbb24f90fc).

comments.author: atqamar-agent
comments.body:
🤖 Snowball performance experiments can complete without checkpoint export

Snowball completed two async Megatron updates through the new metrics-only path on 32 learner + 8 rollout H100s. All five training tasks and the Marin coordinator succeeded. A separate CPU audit verified the durable step-2 result, finished [W&B history](https://wandb.ai/dogml/marin-async-non-agentic-rl/runs/ggsnriwh), and absence of native-checkpoint and HF-export directories.

Direct Finelog queries verified 256 consumed responses, publications 0–2, an empty terminal buffer, and zero reported telemetry loss across five node execution IDs. The token ledger balanced: 191,087 generated = 126,951 consumed + 64,136 discarded at termination. Core RL time was 98.4 seconds. This two-update, 512-token gate qualifies completion and accounting; the short horizon makes prefetched work a large share of its token budget.

Marin now exposes metrics-only training, native-checkpoint training, and a separate HF export stage. Export retries use the recorded checkpoint and source revision without repeating training. The existing model-producing API composes training and export. The duplicate final evaluation is also fixed. Implementation: [MarinSkyRL7160a11e](https://github.com/marin-community/MarinSkyRL/commit/7160a11ecd7485aac9efbf5f3206f9ff289b199d), pinned by [Marindf8986724a](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/df8986724a). Launcher tests: 383 passed; Marin RL tests: 32 passed, with additional focused trainer/export checks.

The earlier Snowball25 export ultimately encountered an Iris completion failure. A read-only audit verified its 39 HF shards and index, but its combined terminal manifest was absent. That failure motivated separating training success from export completion.

Reviewing how the baseline was selected helped calibrate the next experiments:

- **32 learner GPUs** came from the existing Snowball smoke preset's FSDP2 memory layout. We retained that allocation while qualifying Megatron; no allocation sweep has established that 32 is necessary or optimal.
- **8 rollout GPUs** came from the existing node-sized expert-parallel serving layout. The 4:1 ratio was a compatibility starting point.
- **2,048 response tokens** was the planned increase for longer qualification. The earlier 512-token gate's 81–82% length stops supported increasing it; the 25-update run still had 17.4% length stops at 2,048. Those observations motivate testing 4,096, with answer completeness and evaluation quality deciding the budget.

Next: calibrate the response budget and common evaluation protocol, including a full-update memory gate at the larger cap. Then establish Snowball sync/async controls and test publication cadence before expanding inference capacity: the 25-update run attributed 56.2% of steady core time to publication. Promising GPU allocations will follow those measurements.

The comparison endpoint is less elapsed time and fewer allocated H100 GPU-hours at comparable held-out reward. A matched-publication-cadence control will distinguish savings from overlap and savings from publishing weights less often. Useful consumed work and discarded work will accompany utilization measurements.
